title-group.article-title: The Efficacy and Toxicity of CNS Prophylaxis in Diffuse Large B‐Cell Lymphoma (CLSG‐CNS‐01): A Randomized, Multicenter, Prospective Phase 3 Trial

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: The randomized, multicenter, prospective Phase 3 trial (NCT02777736) evaluated central nervous system (CNS) prophylaxis using either intravenous (i.v.) or intrathecal (i.t.) methotrexate (MTX) in diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Treatment consisted of six cycles of R‐CHOP + 2xR or DA‐EPOCH‐R + 2xR. Patients with intermediate or high‐risk CNS International Prognostic Index (CNS‐IPI) were randomized to receive CNS prophylaxis with either 2 doses of MTX 3 g/m2 i.v. (arm A) or 6 doses of MTX 12 mg i.t. (arm B). Patients with low‐risk CNS‐IPI did not receive MTX prophylaxis (arm C). The primary objective was to compare the cumulative incidence of CNS relapse between arms A and B. Secondary objectives included evaluation of overall response rate (ORR), complete remission rate (CRR), progression‐free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and treatment‐related safety across all arms. Between 7/2015 and 5/2024, a total of 100 patients were enrolled: 30 in arm A, 31 in arm B, and 39 in arm C. ORR did not differ among arms (p = 0.20). During a median follow‐up of 54.9 months, CNS relapses were observed in three patients who had received MTX prophylaxis‐one in arm A and two in arm B. The 5‐year cumulative incidence of CNS relapse was 0% in arm A and 8.7% in arm B (p = 0.72). However, due to the small sample size, the primary endpoint results are inconclusive. Median PFS was comparable between arms A and B (HR 0.66, p = 0.20). MTX i.v. was associated with a significantly higher grade ≥ 3 neutropenia (p = 0.0003) and infection (p = 0.0063). The higher infection rate contributed to a worse 5‐year OS in arm A versus B (47.2% vs. 72.4%, HR 0.46, p = 0.04). Conclusion: our trial faced limitations due to a low number of randomized participants, making the interpretation of results challenging. A larger, international randomized trial is necessary to determine the benefit of CNS prophylaxis.

sec.p: Keywords: CNS prophylaxis, CNS relapse, CNS‐IPI, diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma, methotrexate

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: CNS progression or relapse in patients with DLBCL is associated with a median survival of 2–5 months after CNS diagnosis [1]. In the context of immunochemotherapy with rituximab, the CNS‐IPI was formulated, identifying following risk factors: age ≥ 60 years, an ECOG performance status ≥ 2, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) beyond the reference range, involvement of ≥ 2 extranodal sites, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and kidney and/or adrenal involvement [2]. The CNS‐IPI defines three risk groups based on the number of risk factors, that are associated with different 2‐year rate of CNS relapse: 0.8% for low‐risk (0–1 risk factor), 3.9% for intermediate‐risk (two to three risk factors), and 12% for high‐risk (four to six risk factors) [2]. However, the CNS‐IPI does not account for the activated B‐cell subtype of DLBCL [3], high grade B‐cell lymphomas with c‐MYC and BCL2 rearrangements [4] or various extranodal sites associated with higher risk of CNS relapse, such as testicular, bone marrow, uterine or breast involvement [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Currently, the best strategy for CNS prophylaxis remains undefined. Several retrospective studies have failed to confirm a benefit from CNS prophylaxis using MTX i.t. or high doses of MTX (HD MTX) i.v. ≥ 3 g/m2, partly due to inconsistencies in defining risk groups that received prophylaxis [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. Randomized Phase 2 trials of the International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group (IELSG) showed a reduction in CNS relapses in primary testicular lymphoma: the IELSG10 trial combined R‐CHOP with four doses of i.t. MTX followed by radiotherapy to the contralateral testis [17], while IELSG30 used R‐CHOP with four doses of i.t. liposomal cytarabine, followed by two cycles of MTX 1.5 g/m2 i.v. and radiotherapy to the contralateral testis [18]. Several retrospective studies noted benefits of HD MTX [19, 20]. Boehme et al. proposed that CNS prophylaxis should be implemented early in treatment [21]. Wilson et al. found no difference in CNS relapse rates between intercalated HD MTX and HD MTX administered at the end of an anthracycline‐based regimen treatment. However, they observed increased treatment delays when HD MTX was given as an intercalated dose [15]. This randomized, multicenter, prospective Phase 3 trial CLSG‐CNS‐01 (registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02777736) compares the efficacy of CNS prophylaxis with HD MTX i.v. and MTX i.t. in systemic DLBCL.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: All patients provided informed written consent to participate in the CLSG‐CNS‐01 trial for CNS prophylaxis using MTX. The research adhered to legal and institutional ethical standards, having received approvals from local ethics committees at six participating sites and the multicentric ethics committee at Fakultni nemocnice Kralovske Vinohrady in Prague, Czech Republic (reference KH/14/5/2015, dated February 4, 2015). This trial was conducted following the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines.

Eligible participants were patients with newly diagnosed systemic DLBCL aged 18–70 years (extended to 72 years after the amendment on June 3, 2016) who had intermediate or high‐risk CNS‐IPI [2]. Patients with testicular involvement received a more complex CNS prophylaxis [17, 18] and were excluded from this trial. Patients with initial CNS involvement, primary mediastinal B‐cell lymphoma, HIV‐positive status, active hepatitis B or C infections, or with other serious comorbidities were also not eligible for this trial. Patients classified with low‐risk CNS‐IPI were assigned to the control arm without CNS prophylaxis to evaluate safety, PFS and OS. Pathology reports underwent a centralized review by accredited hematopathologists.

The standard diagnostic and relapse workup comprised evaluating Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, conducting a physical examination, performing laboratory tests and carrying out bone marrow biopsy. Imaging studies included positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was analyzed using flow cytometry, cytological and biochemical assessments. PET/CT scans were conducted following three chemotherapy cycles for arms B and C, after the first intercalated HD MTX cycle in arm A and upon completion of the first‐line treatment across all arms, as depicted in Figure 1.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: The systemic immunochemotherapy protocol included either six cycles of R‐CHOP followed by two additional cycles of rituximab (375 mg/m2 i.v.) every 3 weeks [22], or six cycles of DA‐EPOCH‐R with the same subsequent rituximab schedule [23]. Dosage adjustments for subsequent cycles were made as previously described [23]. Patients undergoing DA‐EPOCH‐R were included in the trial with CNS prophylaxis, given that the CNS relapse rates were not significantly different from those treated with R‐CHOP [24]. Patients at intermediate or high risk for CNS relapse were randomly assigned (in a 1:1 ratio) to one of two CNS prophylaxis regimens. The first group (arm A) received two doses of HD MTX 3 g/m2 via a three‐hour intravenous infusion. The second group (arm B) received six doses of MTX 12 mg i.t. per dose. In arm A, the first dose of HD MTX was administered alongside rituximab on day 22 of the third cycle of R–CHOP or DA‐EPOCH‐R, with a 14–days interval before the subsequent systemic immunochemotherapy cycle. The second HD MTX dose was given in combination with rituximab on day 22 of the sixth cycle of R–CHOP or DA–EPOCH–R. Patients in arm B received MTX 12 mg i.t. on day 1 of each R–CHOP or DA–EPOCH–R cycle. Low‐risk patients for CNS relapse were not randomized into the CNS prophylaxis and were allocated into arm C, Figure 1. All patients received standard supportive care, including hydration, antiemetics, antimicrobial prophylaxis, granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor, and blood component therapy, in accordance with the local protocols of each participating center.

sec.title: Objectives and Endpoints
sec.p: Primary objective was to evaluate and compare the cumulative incidence of CNS relapse (primary endpoint) between arms A and B within the predefined analysis period. CNS relapse was characterized by new evidence of lymphoma affecting the brain or spinal cord, as determined by MRI, or the detection of monoclonal B‐cells indicating lymphoma involvement in CSF. In cases of suspected CNS relapse, a brain biopsy and additional CSF analyses were recommended.

Secondary objectives and endpoints included comparison of ORR, CRR, PFS both within and outside the CNS, OS, and treatment safety across all arms. Treatment safety was evaluated using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) Version 4.0.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The primary objective hypothesized, that the cumulative incidence of CNS relapse would be 0% in arm A (HD MTX i.v.) and 6% in arm B (MTX i.t.) after a 1–year follow‐up period. To detect this difference with a significance level α adjusted to 5% and a statistical power of 80%, a total of 320 participants were required with 160 patients in each of arms A and B. Additionally, the anticipated enrollment for the arm C was projected to be 180 patients. The cumulative incidence of CNS lymphoma relapse was calculated from the date of systemic DLBCL diagnosis to the occurrence of CNS lymphoma relapse, with evaluations conducted at 1, 2 and 5 years of follow‐up. These assessments were conducted in accordance with an amendment dated March 23, 2020. The comparison of cumulative CNS relapse incidence between patients treated with HD MTX i.v. and those treated with MTX i.t. (the primary objective) was carried out using the Kaplan‐Meier method, with survival curves assessed through the log‐rank test.

Analyses of secondary objectives and endpoints were amended after the trial termination to avoid misinterpretation of statistically inconclusive results. PFS and OS were defined using established criteria: PFS was measured from the date of diagnosis until the first confirmed evidence of relapse/progression, or death from any cause, while OS was calculated from the date of diagnosis to either the date of the last follow‐up or death from any cause. Both OS and PFS were evaluated using the Kaplan‐Meier method, however, log‐rank tests were not conducted. Comparisons of CRR and ORR between randomized arms A an B are presented solely in descriptive terms.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between June 16, 2015, and May 21, 2024, a total of 102 patients were enrolled in the trial. Of these, two patients were excluded: one due to a revised diagnosis of marginal zone lymphoma, and another who withdrew consent for CNS prophylaxis. A total of 30 patients were randomly assigned to arm A, 31 to arm B, and 39 low‐risk patients received no CNS prophylaxis (arm C), as shown in Figure 1. The baseline characteristics of the studied population are provided in Table 1. The median patient age was 61 years (range: 27‐72), with 54% being male. Key baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between the randomized arms A and B. FISH analyses of lymphoma samples were performed in only a subset of patients, so their impact on CNS relapse was not evaluated in this trial. DA‐EPOCH–R was administered to one patient in arm A, three in arm B and one in arm C; all others received R–CHOP. In arm A, 21 of the 30 patients completed the full systemic immunochemotherapy and two cycles of HD MTX i.v., while 8 patients did not receive the second HD MTX i.v. dose and two of these also failed to complete all R–CHOP cycles due to treatment toxicity (details in Figure 1 and Table 2). In arm B, 29 out of 31 patients completed systemic immunochemotherapy, but there were two early deaths–one due to disease progression and another caused by COVID‐19 infection. Of these patients, 26 completed six doses of MTX i.t. and four discontinued after 5 doses due to post‐puncture headaches, Figure 1. In arm C, three out of 39 patients discontinued their planned immunochemotherapy because of COVID‐19 pneumonia. Specifically, one patient missed the sixth cycle of R–CHOP, while two others did not receive the eighth cycle of rituximab, Figure 1.

sec.p: CNS relapse occurred in three patients (3%) at a median follow‐up of 54.9 months (range 6.2–110.9). These relapses occurred in patients who had received full systemic immunochemotherapy and CNS prophylaxis. Details include: one intermediate‐risk patient who received six cycles of R–CHOP+2R and two doses of HD MTX i.v.; one high‐risk patient was treated with six cycles of DA–EPOCH–R+2R and six doses of MTX i.t.; and one intermediate‐risk patient who received six cycles of R–CHOP+2R and six doses of MTX i.t. Isolated CNS relapse was observed after 5.2 years in one patient after initiation of treatment including HD MTX i.v. prophylaxis. Additionally, two CNS and systemic relapses occurred at 0.77 and 2.2 years after starting systemic treatment and MTX i.t. prophylaxis. The 1‐, 2‐, and 5‐year cumulative incidences of CNS relapses for arms A (0%, 0%, 0%), B (3.7%, 3.7%, 8.77%), and C (0%, 0%, 0%) are presented in Figure 2. A comparison of the 5‐year cumulative incidences of CNS relapse between randomized arms A and B showed no statistically significant difference (0% vs. 8.7%; HR: 1.52 [95% CI: 0.15–14.80], p = 0.72). The ORR was comparable across arms A, B, and C (83.30% vs. 83.80% vs. 94.80%, p = 0.20). The CRR showed no statistically significant differences among the three groups, reported as 63.30% for arm A, 74.19% for arm B, and 84.62% for arm C (p = 0.12, as outlined in Table 2). Following the first intercalated intravenous administration of high‐dose methotrexate (HD MTX), a median delay of 7 days (range: 0–21 days) to the next cycle of immunochemotherapy was observed due to adverse events. There were 17 cases of DLBCL relapse in arm A. The median, as well as the 1‐, 2‐, and 5‐year PFS rates across all treatment arms, are illustrated in Figure 3A.

sec.p: A total of 29 patients died: 16 in arm A, 10 in arm B, and 3 in arm C. The causes of death are detailed in Table 2. During the COVID‐19 pandemic, 6 patients (4 from arm A and 2 from arm B) died at home, and the cause of death could not be determined. The median, as well as 1‐, 2‐, and 5‐year OS rates across all treatment arms, are illustrated in Figure 3B. CNS prophylaxis using HD MTX was associated with a lower 5‐year OS in arm A compared to arm B (47.2% vs. 72.4%).

Grade ≥ 3 adverse events per patient are summarized in Table 3. The use of any CNS prophylaxis led to an increase in grade ≥ 3 neutropenia and anemia compared to the no‐prophylaxis arm. Although arm A showed the highest rate of grade ≥ 3 infections, the small number of patients in arms A and B limits definitive conclusion.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This randomized Phase 3 trial demonstrated a low incidence of CNS relapse (3%) over a median follow‐up period of 54.9 months. The cumulative incidences of CNS relapse at 1, 2, and 5 years showed no significant differences between HD MTX i.v. and MTX i.t. as prophylaxis in patients with high‐risk and intermediate‐risk CNS‐IPI. However, the small number of randomized patients limits the interpretation of the primary objective. We were unable to enroll the target of 160 patients in arms A and B, even with an extended enrollment period. The primary factors contributing to the low accrual included the exclusion of patients with testicular involvement, competition with Phase 3 trials introducing innovative drugs, the impact of the COVID‐19 pandemic, limited interest from patients and physicians in participating in an academic trial, expected challenges with methotrexate i.t. application, and the requirement for hospitalization to administer HD MTX i.v. Some of above mentioned issues may be addressed in a large international trial comparing added CNS prophylaxis versus no CNS prophylaxis and incorporating patient stratification based on molecular techniques as an important component of the trial. A large international trial involves significant costs, demanding substantial funding to support advanced administrative infrastructure and staffing needs.

A key strength of our trial lies in the long‐term follow‐up. Based on our findings, future trials should aim to include a follow‐up period of at least a similar duration. Exclusion of patients with testicular involvement reduced the enrollment of patients at the highest risk and this may partly explain the low overall CNS relapse rate observed. This exclusion represents a limitation of the trial. Our patients with testicular involvement outside of the trial received four to six doses of MTX 12 mg i.t. in combination with R‐CHOP chemotherapy, followed by two doses of HD MTX i.v. 3 g/m2 and radiotherapy to the contralateral testis. A retrospective analysis from the Czech Lymphoma Study Group Registry reported a 5‐year cumulative incidence of CNS relapse of 4.5% in primary testicular lymphoma and 12.1% in patients with advanced‐stage DLBCL involving the testicles [6]. These findings suggest that this is a distinct group of patients, which could bias general results if included into the trial.

Yahng et al. conducted a phase III randomized study that compared the efficacy of prophylactic MTX 15 mg i.t. (73 patients) and MTX 3 g/m2 i.v. (69 patients) in patients with DLBCL at high risk for CNS relapse and found no significant difference in the 2‐year cumulative incidence of CNS relapse between the MTX i.t. arm (5.5%) and the MTX i.v. arm (4.9%), p = 0.749 [25]. Although this study was larger than ours, the data still may not have been sufficiently powered to definitively reject the null hypothesis. A metaanalysis of 36 studies that retrospectively evaluated CNS prophylaxis found no evidence that any of the approaches—whether HD MTX i.v. (with or without cytarabine), MTX i.t., or lenalidomide—reduced the rate of CNS relapse in high‐risk patients [26]. This metaanalysis also revealed that intercalated HD MTX i.v. did not significantly reduce the risk of CNS relapse (p = 0.67). However, the inclusion of rituximab improved control of systemic disease [26]. The impact of intercalated HD MTX i.v. on CNS relapse could not be assessed in our trial, as only a single patient receiving HD MTX i.v. experienced a CNS relapse during the extended follow‐up period. Other authors recommend to defer the delivery of HD MTX after completion of systemic immunochemotherapy as this approach does not increase the CNS relapse risk [15]. A metaanalysis of seven observational studies involving 1661 patients who received HD MTX i.v. Further confirmed that this prophylaxis neither prevented nor significantly reduced the risk of CNS relapse. Additionally, it showed no survival benefit for patients with high‐risk DLBCL [27]. The impact of DA‐EPOCH‐R on CNS relapse was not analyzed in our trial due to the low number of patients in all arms treated with this modality. MTX i.t. is insufficient for CNS prophylaxis and CNS relapses after MTX i.t. occurred relatively early post‐treatment and concomitantly with systemic relapses in our trial. Isolated CNS relapse after HD MTX i.v. was detected later during the follow‐up. CNS‐IPI has limitations and modern diagnostics like circulating tumor DNA [28, 29, 30, 31], and better understanding of DLBCL biology [32, 33, 34] could probably have potential to refine stratification of CNS‐IPI. FISH analysis, cell‐of‐origin data and molecular characterization are increasingly recognized as relevant for CNS relapse risk, however, these data were available for only a minority or none of our patients and it represents a limitation of our trial. The molecular stratification (e.g., COO, double‐hit status, ctDNA) should be integrated into future studies exploring CNS prophylaxis. Recent evidence also suggests that certain biological factors, such as MYD88 and CD79b mutations, may increase the risk of delayed CNS relapse [35]. Since these molecular data were not assessed in our trial, it is possible that unrecognized biological heterogeneity affected outcomes. Furthermore, the fact that the CNS relapse observed in arm A was isolated (without systemic progression) could hypothetically indicate better systemic disease control with HD MTX prophylaxis.

Despite the fact, that intercalated HD MTX i.v. in arm A postponed the next cycle of systemic immunochemotherapy (median 7 days), the median PFS did not differ significantly between arms A and B (p = 0.20) and between high‐and intermediate‐risk patients in both arms (p = 0.86 and p = 0.18). Out of 30 patients who received intercalated HD MTX i.v., eight were unable to receive the second dose of CNS prophylaxis due to MTX‐related toxicity. Additionally, two early toxic deaths following the intercalated dose of HD MTX i.v. administration negatively impacted the 1‐year OS in our trial. HD MTX i.v. (intercalated and at the end of R‐CHOP) led to a proportional rise in grade ≥ 3 infections (30% compared to 6.4%) and negatively impacted the 5‐year OS (47.2% vs. 72.4%). Wilson et al. conducted a retrospective analysis of 1384 patients who underwent HD MTX for CNS prophylaxis, administered either intercalated during R‐CHOP or R‐CHOP‐like therapy (n = 749) or at the end of treatment (n = 635). The study found that giving HD MTX after completing R‐CHOP did not reduce the risk of CNS relapse but was associated with significantly lower toxicity compared to intercalated administration [15]. HD MTX toxicity observed in our trial supports the strategy of administering this prophylactic treatment after completing first‐line immunochemotherapy. This approach could minimize MTX toxicity without compromising efficacy. Several deaths during the Covid‐19 pandemic had undocumented causes, potentially introducing bias into the OS analysis and highlighting another limitation of the trial. The negative impact of HD MTX on treatment related death is also confirmed by metaanalysis of 36 studies that tested CNS prophylaxis [26]. In our trial, the median OS was comparable between intermediate‐risk and high‐risk patients in arm A (HR 1.51, p = 0.36). However, in arm B, high‐risk patients experienced significantly worse median OS compared to intermediate‐risk patients (HR 4.69, p = 0.0097), primarily due to deaths linked to DLBCL relapse.

Conclusions: The major limitation of our trial was low number of randomized patients. This limits sensitivity of the analyses and does not allow definitive conclusions. If CNS prophylaxis is required, it is important to explore less toxic and more effective treatment options. Conducting a large, randomized international trial will be essential to determine the benefits of CNS prophylaxis.
